title: Prompt, Patch, Prove
thesis: An agentic coding model can analyze closed firmware and produce testable binary-level repairs for known vulnerabilities, giving defenders a way to deploy interim fixes before the vendor ships, provided every claim is independently verified because the model's first patches were incomplete.
summary: Tim de Waal, a security researcher at OpenAI speaking from a personal account, argued that AI can now reverse and repair binary firmware cheaply enough that defenders should do it themselves. He framed the problem first: one device contains several firmware layers, including third-party chip firmware that even the manufacturer cannot see; the time from disclosure to weaponized exploit has fallen from about 2.3 years in 2018 to about 10 hours; and vendors need weeks to months for triage, supplier fixes, QA, signing and rollout, after which users may never update. He then showed a lab experiment on an authorized ASUS RT-BE82U router running build 39099. Using one model in a bare Codex install, with no extra skills and no open-weight models, he had it download the firmware, set up an emulated lab, confirm two published authenticated vulnerabilities (a command injection, CVE-2025-15101, and a SQL injection, CVE-2026-11851), repair each in the binary, test on a real device, and build a flashable image. The whole exercise used about 7 percent of a weekly Pro allowance, roughly $48 at API rates. The model's first patches were incomplete: one dropped a stack-canary check and the SQL fix was bypassable, which independent testing and assembly comparison caught. He closed with a device-in-the-loop workflow and Q&A on emulation, verification and mitigations.
argument: Firmware on critical and home devices is opaque to buyers, includes third-party code the vendor itself cannot see, and has relied on obscurity that AI-assisted reverse engineering removes.
Weaponization time has collapsed while vendor fix and user update cycles remain slow, so defenders face a long exposure window.
A single agentic model with a plain prompt and a lab can unpack firmware, confirm known flaws, propose binary patches and rebuild a flashable image for about $48 of usage.
The model's patches cannot be trusted on its say-so: both first-pass repairs had gaps that only independent checks, assembly diffing and broader negative tests found.

The practical protocol is device-in-the-loop: operator sets a goal, the model patches, an adversary step tries to break the patch, and failures return to the model until the patch passes both attack and normal-behavior tests.
Vendors still need to apply known mitigations such as least privilege and access control, since the models do not remove the need for defense in depth.

claims.claim: Average time to weaponize a vulnerability fell from about 2.3 years in 2018 to about 10 hours now.
claims.evidence: Chart attributed to the zerodayclock project, labelled UK AI Safety Institute, April 2026, based on 3,536 CVE-exploit pairs.

claims.claim: The full exercise, from firmware download to a repaired flashable image for two CVEs, used about 7 percent of a weekly Pro allowance, roughly $48 API-equivalent.
claims.evidence: Speaker's own usage figure; slide notes the figure includes a 2x fast rate. Model GPT-6 Sol at extra-high reasoning, bare Codex, no added skills.

claims.claim: The model confirmed two published authenticated flaws on the lab router and produced proof scripts, which the speaker re-ran himself rather than trusting the model's report.
claims.evidence: Pre-recorded terminal demos for each CVE showing the vulnerable behavior, including positive and negative controls for the SQL case.

claims.claim: For the command injection, the model's repair rejected a set of dangerous characters before the shell calls, and the patched handler lost the original stack-canary check.
claims.evidence: Side-by-side original and patched assembly from Binary Ninja on a slide; speaker judged no direct overflow remained because the write is bounded and accepted the risk.

claims.claim: The model's first SQL injection fix, which only rejected quote characters, was incomplete and needed several re-prompts.
claims.evidence: Slide and speaker showing a column-name style input that still matched every row.

claims.claim: The final SQL repair compiled a small helper in C, linked it, appended 1,684 bytes to the library, and redirected the original formatting call to it through a trampoline.
claims.evidence: Step-by-step diagram with addresses and payload size on slides, and a speaker walkthrough.

claims.claim: A model-built hash-locked patch and rebuilt firmware package could be flashed so the fix survives reboot.
claims.evidence: Stated in the prompt and description; a post-patch re-run of the proof scripts is shown failing to exploit.

claims.claim: Third-party chipset firmware shared across devices is a good place to look, and the model can use public filings to find cheaper or easier devices with the same chipset.
claims.evidence: Speaker suggestion with an example workflow; no results shown.

claims.claim: Emulation speeds iteration but cannot replace real hardware for effects such as cache behavior, multi-core interaction, and inter-process communication.

frameworks.name: Device-in-the-loop firmware repair loop
frameworks.description: Four lanes: operator provides exact firmware build and research goal; model unpacks firmware, analyzes attack paths and proposes or revises a patch; an adversary step, optionally in emulation, tries to break the patch with bypasses and edge cases; the physical device runs attacks and normal-behavior tests, and failures and traces feed back into analysis.

frameworks.name: Layers of one device's firmware
frameworks.description: User space (vendor web app and libraries), kernel and modules including drivers, boot and trust (signed boot, verification, rollback), third-party SoC, and on-chip firmware for radio, switch and neural processing unit.

frameworks.name: Prompting protocol
frameworks.description: Ask for scripts that prove or disprove each claimed vulnerability, require no regression and provable fixes, prototype on the device first, build a flashable image with a version string that marks the fix, and treat model-requested verification as still needing independent testing.

slide_only: Slide gives the model setup: extra-high reasoning, Daybreak Blue access, personal Pro plan, bare Codex with no additional skills installed.
The first prompt slide says to find the firmware, download it to a separate directory, set up QEMU, and notes that a local lab-only isolated environment is wanted.
The verification prompt slide asks for proof-of-concept scripts that prove or disprove that the CVEs are present.

The repair prompt slide asks for no regression in functionality and provable fixes, prototyping on the unit first, then creating and flashing a new image whose version indicates the fix, framed as a goal.
A slide contrasts disabling a vulnerable handler with repairing it, and the speaker chose repair for the exercise.

A slide labelled 'What the model missed' lists the removed stack-canary check (found by comparing original and patched assembly, accepted as a known risk) and the SQL filter bypass (found through broader query testing, needing extra rounds).
demos: Pre-recorded demo confirming the command-injection flaw on the lab router running build 39099 and showing the resulting privileged process listing.
Pre-recorded demo of the SQL injection with positive and negative controls and a test-data cleanup step.
Live demo of the patched router: the proof script fails to exploit the command injection and reports an inconclusive result, and the SQL test is started against the patched build.

quotes.text: It's no longer about prompt engineering. The model is super capable, and six months from now it's going to look totally different with a different model.
quotes.speaker: Tim de Waal

quotes.text: I don't want to explicitly trust the LLM. If it says something's successful, I actually want to check.
quotes.speaker: Tim de Waal

quotes.text: We know the right things to do, and vendors need to go and do it. You should never have a single point of failure.
quotes.speaker: Tim de Waal

offense: Both repaired CVEs require authenticated management access and are published issues, chosen so the talk would not disclose new zero-days.
The speaker argued that attackers can analyze firmware in hours, and that shared chipsets make a bug in one cheap device likely to matter on others.
defense: Run an interim binary patch workflow for devices where the vendor fix is slow: analyze the exact build, patch minimally, test on hardware, and flash a version-marked image.
Require proof scripts and negative controls for every claimed vulnerability and every claimed fix, and re-run them yourself.
Diff original and patched assembly or equivalent to catch regressions such as a removed stack-canary check.
Use broad negative tests for injection fixes, since a model's first filter may only block the obvious input.
Keep standard mitigations in place: least privilege (do not run the web server as root), mandatory access control, and no single point of failure.
Inventory third-party firmware and chipsets in your estate, since they are shared attack surface.
takeaways: Treat embedded and network-edge firmware as in scope for in-house analysis rather than waiting for vendor advisories, using an isolated lab and authorized devices.
Plan for much shorter exploit windows and decide in advance who can authorize an interim patch when no vendor fix exists.
Build a verification gate for any AI-produced patch: independent tests, assembly diff, regression suite, and a human sign-off on accepted risks.
Ask suppliers which chipsets and third-party firmware sit inside purchased devices and how fast they can ship signed updates.
Budget is not the barrier: a two-CVE repair exercise cost about $48 in usage, so effort should go into test harnesses and approval process.
limits: Only two known, authenticated, string-handling vulnerabilities were repaired on one consumer router, chosen on purpose to be simple.
The speaker said the command-injection repair removed the stack-canary check and that he accepted that risk after review.
Emulation does not capture hardware effects, and complex exploit development on the vendor's own flagship devices may need a real device.
The speaker said exploit development under the restricted trusted-access program is tricky and gave no tips for finding variants the model missed.
critique: The evidence is a single lab run on two simple, published bugs, so claims about repairing arbitrary firmware or scaling the approach are not supported by data in the talk.
The cost figure is from the speaker's own allowance accounting, and the talk does not say whether it includes his time or the manual verification.
Hot-patching production devices with unsigned or self-built images raises supportability, warranty and update-chain questions that were not addressed.
Both first patches were incomplete, which supports the case for verification gates rather than for model autonomy.
The speaker works at the company that makes the model and used a trusted-access program, so the workflow may not be reproducible without that access or on other models.
The time-to-weaponization chart's methodology is not explained, so the 10-hour figure should be treated as indicative.
qa: Q: Did emulation with QEMU teach anything? A: It speeds iteration and avoids reboot waits, and the model can run binaries in user-mode emulation; but cache coherency, multi-core interaction, heap-related second-order effects and inter-process communication need real hardware.

Q: Was using a personal account deliberate? A: Yes, to show what anyone with the trusted-access program can do; he used only Codex with no skills, no open-weight models, and the model mostly used standard disassembly tools.

Q: Thoughts on enforcing authorization layers at firmware level? A: The industry knows the right mitigations and vendors must apply them; no single control is enough, and access control should stop a code-execution bug from becoming a root shell.
Q: How were exploit variants and patches verified? A: He relied on the model's verification loop but manually checked everything to catch hallucination.
Q: Tips for finding variants the model missed? A: None specific; exploit work under the restricted access program is tricky, and this case was a simple injection.

key_frames.caption: Attacker versus vendor timeline: exploitation in days against weeks to months for a vendor fix, with the interim patch window highlighted.
Model, access and setup slide: model, reasoning level, bare Codex, 7 percent of weekly allowance, about $48.
Repair and test prompt: no regression, provable fixes, prototype on the device first, then build a flashable image.
What the model missed: a removed stack-canary check and a bypassable SQL filter, and how each was caught.
Device-in-the-loop firmware research workflow across operator, model, adversary and physical device lanes.

signal.reason: Practical defender-side workflow with failure cases shown and a clear cost figure; the evidence is one lab run on two simple bugs.

caveats: Summary-level record: exploit mechanics deliberately not recorded.
Auto-captions garble the speaker name as 'Tim Daval' and the model as 'GPT 6 Soul'; the slides give Tim de Waal and GPT-6 Sol.
The first-prompt slide names firmware build 39033 and a correction to 39099; the transcript does not mention the first number.

The slide's chart attribution reads UK AI Safety Institute, April 2026, and the zerodayclock.com footer; the transcript says 'zero day clock' and that the graphic may have been removed from the site, which was not verified.
The transcript says the command-injection demo showed root access and that the ID command was missing; the slide screenshots show a privileged process listing rather than the missing command.
Final live demo of the patched router is only partly visible in captured frames.
